quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage defines the core terminology system used throughout the volume, giving readers the vocabulary needed to follow all subsequent analytical discussions.

quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage establishes the foundational distinction between an event and an episode — two structural categories central to how the method analyzes melodic and harmonic material.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
an event can be diatonically

quotes.why_load_bearing: This rule teaches how events behave under diatonic transposition and flags that intervallic identity can collapse distinct transpositions, a key constraint for voice-leading analysis.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
an episode can be diatonically
transposed to create 6 other
episodes, where each corresponds
to a different mode.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This rule establishes the modal correspondence of episodic transpositions, connecting the episode concept directly to the seven diatonic modes.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
We naturally tend to think of events as being shorter, while episodes are longer.

This is true much of the time. However, it is quite possible to have a very long event and

a relatively short episode.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This clarification prevents the common misconception that length is definitional for events vs. episodes, keeping the distinction grounded in pitch-content rather than duration.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
My suggestion for a suitable name for this chord would be: G [sus4].
That means a G Major triad with 4 suspended for 3. I will grant you that C2 is shorter, but
Ineed to ask, "How many musicans understand this terminology?" (I think not many...)
Also, you need to consider the potential problems that would occur with other names that
are more complicated: B Diminished triad [no b3rd] add b9. {This is much easier to name
as F [sus#4].} Or how about: E Minor triad [no b3rd] add b9. {This is much easier to name
as B diminished [sus4].}
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage gives the author's explicit naming convention and rationale for stacked-fourths chords, including worked examples of how sus4 notation handles otherwise unwieldy chord descriptions.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
NAMES FOR 4-PART 4THS

This is fairly simple: Sus 4 Chords...[I think it's the best way to go...]

Your other option would be: C Major 7th [no 5] substitute 4 for the missing 5th.

quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage establishes the naming rule for 4-part stacked-fourth chords and explicitly rejects the more cumbersome alternative, clarifying the author's preferred terminological approach.
